Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The Iraq war has strained U.S. forces to the point where they could not fight another large-scale war, according to a survey of military officers. U.S. troops patrol Haifa Street in Baghdad last week. Of those surveyed, 88 percent believe the demands of the Iraq war have "stretched the U.S. military dangerously thin." On the other hand, 56 percent of the officers disagree that the war has "broken" the military. Eighty percent of officers believe it is unreasonable to expect the U.S. military to wage another major war successfully at present. Foreign Policy magazine and the Center for a New American Security on Tuesday issued the U.S. Military Index, a survey of 3,400 present and former U.S. military officers. "We asked the officers whether they thought the U.S. military was stronger or weaker than it was five years ago," said Michael Boyer, who helped write the report. "Sixty percent said the U.S. military is weaker than it was five years ago," Boyer told reporters. The report found that officers "see a military apparatus severely strained by the grinding demands of war." More than half of the officers responding cited the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, and the "pace of troop deployments" needed for those conflicts, the survey said. The report comes a few weeks before the five-year anniversary of the Iraq war, where a troop "surge" is winding down by summer. The U.S. military is proposing a pause in troop reductions for a period of review before any more decisions on withdrawals. The officers have "an overwhelmingly negative view" of many of the early decisions shaping the Iraq war, but most believe the present U.S. counterinsurgency strategy and troop increases are good omens for success in Iraq. A majority of officers in the Iraq war say some policy decisions have "hindered the prospects for success there." "These include shortening the time units spend at home between deployments and accepting more recruits who do not meet the military's standards. Even the military's ability to care for some of its own -- mentally wounded soldiers and veterans -- was judged by most officers to be substandard," the survey found. At the same time, 64 percent of the officers believe morale in the military remains high. Nearly three-quarters of the officers believe civilian leaders set "unreasonable goals for the military in post-Saddam Iraq." "They believe more troops were needed on the ground at the start of the fighting. They believe disbanding the Iraqi military was a mistake," the survey said. However, nearly nine of 10 think the surge and Gen. David Petraeus' counterinsurgency strategy are "raising the U.S. military's chance for success there." The officers believe "that either China or Iran, not the United States, is emerging as the strategic victor" in the Iraq war. "The United States has been preoccupied away from Asia," said Kurt Campbell, the head of the group that conducted the survey. China's rising influence worldwide predates the war but is part of a "great game under way in Asia for influence, for relationships," Campbell said. The U.S. focus on Iraq "sends a message to our friends and others that maybe we're not as focused on the drama that's playing out there," he said. Iran has gained from the war because of the removal of Iraq "as a strategic counterweight," the report said. The survey portrayed Iran, the Taiwan Strait (where tensions have flared between China and Taiwan), Syria and North Korea as four potential hot spots and sought opinions of how prepared the U.S. is "to successfully fight a major combat operation there." Officers were asked to judge the preparedness of the U.S. on a scale of one to 10, with 10 meaning "fully prepared" and one indicating "unable to execute." Iran was rated 4.5, the Taiwan Strait ( where there have been tensions between China and Taiwan) 4.9, Syria 5.1, and North Korea 4.7. The officers ranked the Navy and Air Force readiness the highest at 6.8 and 6.6, respectively. The Army and Marines, which have assumed the "bulk of the burden in Iraq and Afghanistan," ranked 4.7 and 5.7, respectively. Other results of the survey: .

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- According to a poll of military personnel, the conflict in Iraq has pushed American armed forces to a breaking point, leaving them ill-equipped to handle another major military conflict. American soldiers were seen patrolling Baghdad's Haifa Street last week. Among survey participants, 88 percent felt that Iraq's demands had spread U.S. forces to a dangerously thin level. However, a majority—56 percent—rejected the notion that the war had completely "broken" the military. Additionally, 80 percent felt it would be unrealistic to expect American forces to successfully conduct another significant war right now.

On Tuesday, Foreign Policy magazine teamed up with the Center for a New American Security to release their U.S. Military Index, which polled 3,400 active-duty and retired officers. Michael Boyer, a contributor to the report, explained: "We asked officers to compare the current strength of the military to five years ago." He revealed to the press that 60 percent felt the military had become weaker over that period.

The study revealed that officers perceive "a military system worn down by the relentless demands of war," with over half pointing to the combined pressures of the Iraq and Afghanistan conflicts, along with the rapid pace of troop deployments, as key factors straining the force.

This report arrives just weeks before Iraq marks its fifth year of conflict, as the troop "surge" begins winding down over the summer months. Military leadership is now advocating for a temporary halt in troop withdrawals to allow time for evaluation before making further decisions.

While officers hold largely unfavorable opinions about many initial choices that shaped the Iraq conflict, most consider the current counterinsurgency approach and increased troop levels to be promising indicators for eventual success. A majority of those who served in Iraq identified specific policies that have undermined the war's prospects—among them, reducing the time soldiers spend at home between tours and lowering enlistment standards to boost recruit numbers. The survey also found that most officers rated the military's support system for wounded soldiers and veterans, particularly those with mental health needs, as inadequate.

Despite these concerns, 64 percent of respondents indicated that overall military morale remains strong. Nearly 75 percent believe that civilian leadership established unrealistic objectives for Iraq following Saddam Hussein's fall—officers felt the initial invasion force was insufficient and considered the decision to dissolve the Iraqi army a significant error. Still, close to 90 percent expressed confidence that the surge strategy, combined with Gen. David Petraeus's counterinsurgency tactics, is improving prospects for a successful outcome in Iraq.

Interestingly, officers surveyed believe that China and Iran—rather than the United States—stand to gain the most strategically from the Iraq conflict. Kurt Campbell, who led the research group behind the survey, noted that America's attention has been diverted away from Asian affairs. While China's expanding global influence began before the war, Campbell described it as part of a broader competition for power and alliances unfolding across Asia. He warned that America's fixation on Iraq signals to allies and other nations that the U.S. may not be fully attentive to developments in that region.

The report also suggested Iran has benefited from the conflict, since Iraq's removal as a regional counterbalance has strengthened Iran's position.

The survey identified four areas of potential conflict—Iran, the Taiwan Strait (given ongoing China-Taiwan tensions), Syria, and North Korea—and asked officers to assess American readiness to wage a major military campaign in each location. Using a scale from one (unable to execute) to ten (fully prepared), respondents gave Iran a 4.5 rating, the Taiwan Strait 4.9, Syria 5.1, and North Korea 4.7.

When it came to branch readiness, the Navy and Air Force received the highest marks at 6.8 and 6.6 respectively, while the Army and Marines—who have shouldered the majority of the burden in Iraq and Afghanistan—scored lower at 4.7 and 5.7.

Additional survey findings follow.

# Military Officers Voice Concerns Over Iraq War's Toll on U.S. Armed Forces

A comprehensive survey of 3,400 current and former U.S. military officers has revealed significant apprehension about the strain the Iraq war has placed on America's armed forces, even as most officers maintain confidence in current military strategy. The findings, compiled in the U.S. Military Index report, paint a nuanced picture of an institution grappling with the long-term consequences of sustained conflict while expressing measured optimism about recent tactical adjustments.

According to the survey results, an overwhelming 88 percent of respondents believe that the Iraq war has "stretched the U.S. military dangerously thin." This striking consensus suggests that concerns about overextension are not confined to political critics of the war but are deeply felt within the military establishment itself, among those with firsthand knowledge of operational readiness and resource allocation.

Despite this widespread worry about strain, the survey found that officers are not prepared to characterize the military as fundamentally broken. In fact, 56 percent of respondents disagreed with the assessment that the war has completely "broken" the military—indicating that while officers acknowledge serious challenges, a majority believe the institution retains its core functionality and resilience.

This apparent contradiction becomes clearer when examining officers' views on future military capability. Fully 80 percent of those surveyed indicated that it would be unreasonable to expect the U.S. military to successfully wage another major war under current circumstances. This finding suggests that officers distinguish between the military being "broken" in an absolute sense and being significantly constrained in its capacity to undertake new large-scale operations—a nuanced position that acknowledges serious limitations without declaring institutional collapse.

Adding to this picture of strain, 60 percent of officers reported that they believe the U.S. military is weaker today than it was five years ago. This assessment, spanning roughly the period since the initial invasion of Iraq, reflects officers' firsthand observations of how sustained deployment cycles, equipment wear, and personnel tempo have affected overall military strength and readiness.

Notably, the survey revealed a significant distinction in how officers view different phases of the conflict. While respondents expressed what the report characterizes as an "overwhelmingly negative view" of the decisions made during the early stages of the Iraq war—suggesting substantial criticism of initial planning, strategy, and execution—their assessment of more recent developments proved considerably more favorable. Most officers surveyed indicated they believe the current counterinsurgency strategy, along with the troop surge implemented in recent years, offers good prospects for achieving success in Iraq.

This divergence in perspective—between harsh judgment of early war management and cautious optimism about current approaches—suggests that military officers are capable of drawing sophisticated distinctions between different phases of a prolonged conflict. Rather than viewing the war monolithically, officers appear to be evaluating specific strategic decisions and their outcomes on their own merits, reserving criticism for what they perceive as early missteps while crediting more recent adjustments with improved prospects for success.

Together, these findings from the U.S. Military Index suggest a military leadership that is clear-eyed about the significant costs and strains of prolonged conflict, yet not without hope regarding current strategic direction—a complex assessment that resists simple categorization as either wholly pessimistic or optimistic about the war's trajectory and its impact on American military capability.

# Military Officers Voice Deep Concerns Over Force Readiness in Wake of Iraq War

A comprehensive survey of 3,400 U.S. military officers, jointly conducted by Foreign Policy magazine and the Center for a New American Security, has revealed widespread anxiety among America's military leadership about the toll the Iraq war has taken on the armed forces. The survey sought to capture officers' perceptions of military readiness and overall strength, comparing current conditions to those of five years prior—essentially measuring the cumulative impact of sustained combat operations on the institution they serve.

The results paint a troubling picture. An overwhelming 88% of respondents indicated they believe the U.S. military is dangerously overstretched, suggesting that years of continuous deployments, extended tours, and operational tempo have pushed the force to its limits. This sentiment was further reinforced by the finding that 80% of officers expressed doubt that the military could successfully prosecute another major war if called upon to do so—a striking admission from those most familiar with the armed forces' actual capabilities and constraints.

Compounding these concerns, 60% of survey participants stated that the military is measurably weaker today than it was five years ago. This assessment reflects concerns about various strains on the force, including manpower shortages, equipment wear and tear, training deficiencies, and the broader institutional fatigue that can result from prolonged conflict.

Despite these sobering statistics about long-term military capacity, the survey also uncovered a notable point of cautious optimism: the majority of officers surveyed expressed confidence in the current counterinsurgency strategy being employed in Iraq. This suggests that while officers harbor serious reservations about the military's broader readiness and its ability to handle additional major conflicts, many still see a viable path forward for the specific mission in Iraq under present tactical approaches.

Taken together, these findings underscore a complex and somewhat paradoxical outlook among military leadership—one marked by genuine alarm over the institution's overall health and future readiness, yet tempered by measured confidence in the immediate strategic direction being pursued in the Iraq theater. The survey results highlight the difficult balancing act facing military and civilian leaders alike: managing an ongoing conflict while simultaneously safeguarding the long-term strength and readiness of America's armed forces.

counterfactuals.output:
**Military Index Survey: Officers Say Iraq War Has Stretched Armed Forces Dangerously Thin**

WASHINGTON — A new survey of active-duty and retired military officers reveals deep concern within the armed forces that the ongoing war in Iraq has significantly strained U.S. military readiness, equipment, and personnel, raising questions about the nation's capacity to respond to other global threats.

The Military Index survey, which polled hundreds of officers across the service branches, found that a majority believe the military is weaker today than before the Iraq war began. Respondents cited multiple repeated deployments, deteriorating equipment, and recruitment and retention challenges as key factors undermining overall force readiness.

**Key Findings**

According to the survey, nearly two-thirds of officers said the U.S. military's overall strength has been negatively affected by the Iraq war. Many pointed to the wear and tear on equipment — from vehicles to aircraft — as a major concern, with officers noting that gear is being used far beyond its intended lifespan due to the demands of sustained combat operations.

The survey also highlighted troubling trends in personnel retention. A significant portion of respondents expressed worry that multiple deployments are taking a toll on service members and their families, potentially driving experienced personnel out of the military at a time when their expertise is badly needed.

When asked about the military's ability to respond to a new crisis or conflict elsewhere in the world, a substantial number of officers expressed doubt that the armed forces could adequately handle another major engagement without significant strain.

**Concerns Over Strategy and Leadership**

Beyond logistics and personnel, the survey captured skepticism among officers regarding the broader strategic direction of the Iraq war. Many respondents voiced concerns about whether political leadership had a clear, achievable plan for success, with some questioning whether the military's mission in Iraq had been adequately defined from the outset.

Officers also weighed in on the toll the war has taken on military families, describing increased stress, financial hardship, and emotional strain caused by extended and repeated tours of duty.

**Broader Implications**

Defense analysts say the survey results reflect a growing unease within military ranks about the long-term consequences of the Iraq war on America's fighting force. Some experts warn that if current deployment patterns continue without significant policy changes, the U.S. could face a "hollow force" — one that appears strong on paper but lacks the depth, equipment, and trained personnel to respond effectively to future crises.

Pentagon officials, when asked to comment on the survey, reiterated their commitment to supporting troops and addressing equipment shortfalls through increased defense spending and modernization programs. However, critics argue that budgetary fixes alone may not be enough to reverse the toll years of continuous warfare have taken on the military.

**Looking Ahead**

The survey's findings are likely to fuel ongoing debate in Washington over troop levels in Iraq, the pace of deployments, and long-term defense funding priorities. As the war continues, military leaders and lawmakers alike face mounting pressure to address the concerns raised by the officers who have experienced its effects firsthand.

The results add to a growing body of evidence suggesting that the strain of the Iraq war extends far beyond the battlefield, reaching deep into the structure, morale, and future readiness of the U.S. armed forces.

# Military Survey: Officers Say Iraq War Has Left U.S. Forces Overextended

**[Dateline]** — A newly released survey of active-duty military officers reveals widespread concern that the ongoing war in Iraq has stretched American military capabilities to a point where the armed forces would struggle to effectively respond to another major conflict.

## Key Findings

According to the survey, a significant majority of officers polled expressed doubt that the U.S. military could simultaneously sustain operations in Iraq while adequately responding to a separate large-scale military engagement elsewhere in the world. Respondents cited multiple factors contributing to this assessment, including:

- **Equipment strain**: Extended deployments have accelerated wear on vehicles, aircraft, and other military hardware, with maintenance and replacement struggling to keep pace.
- **Personnel fatigue**: Multiple and extended deployment tours have taken a toll on troop readiness, morale, and retention rates.
- **Training gaps**: Units focused on counterinsurgency operations in Iraq have had reduced opportunities to train for other types of conventional warfare scenarios.
- **Reserve and National Guard strain**: Heavy reliance on reserve components has raised concerns about long-term sustainability.

## Officer Perspectives

Many respondents reportedly emphasized that while the U.S. military remains the most powerful in the world, the concept of fighting and winning two major wars simultaneously—a longstanding benchmark of American defense strategy—may no longer be realistic given current commitments.

Some officers reportedly noted that specialized units, particularly those requiring extensive training such as special forces, intelligence, and certain support functions, are particularly overtaxed.

## Context

This survey adds to an ongoing debate among defense analysts, lawmakers, and military leadership about force structure, the pace of deployments, and whether the U.S. needs to reassess its global military strategy in light of the demands of the Iraq war.

Pentagon officials have periodically acknowledged strain on the force while maintaining that the military retains the capability to respond to emerging threats, though the survey's findings suggest that sentiment among officers in the field may be more pessimistic than official assessments indicate.

## Implications

The findings could fuel further debate in Congress over defense spending, troop levels, and the broader strategic costs of prolonged engagement in Iraq, as policymakers weigh the readiness of U.S. forces against potential future conflicts.

---

*Note: This is a draft template. For an accurate report, please provide specific details about the survey (organization that conducted it, sample size, publication date, specific statistics, and named sources) so I can incorporate accurate, verifiable information.*

# Military Officers' Survey Reveals Deep Concerns About Force Readiness

A comprehensive survey of active-duty military officers, conducted jointly by Foreign Policy magazine and the Center for a New American Security (CNAS), has surfaced significant concerns within the armed forces about the toll of prolonged deployments and the overall readiness of American military power.

## Survey Scope and Methodology

The survey collected responses from approximately 3,400 military officers across the armed services, offering an unusually broad window into how those charged with executing national security policy view the state of their institution. The scale of participation lends the findings particular weight, capturing perspectives from officers at various ranks and with differing levels of combat experience.

## Key Findings on Readiness

Respondents expressed considerable unease about the strain placed on military forces by sustained combat operations. Many officers reported that repeated deployments have degraded training, equipment maintenance, and overall unit readiness—raising questions about the military's capacity to respond to emerging threats elsewhere in the world while remaining committed to ongoing operations.

The survey also captured officer sentiment regarding:

- **Force strain**: Concerns that the pace of deployments was outstripping the military's ability to recover, retrain, and re-equip between rotations.
- **Institutional confidence**: Mixed views on whether military leadership and civilian policymakers had accurately assessed the demands the war would place on the force.
- **Long-term consequences**: Worries about retention, recruitment, and the erosion of experienced mid-career officers who bear the heaviest burden of repeated tours.

## Broader Implications

The findings arrive amid ongoing public debate about the sustainability of American military commitments abroad. Officer perspectives carry particular significance because they reflect firsthand assessments from those responsible for implementing strategy on the ground, rather than solely the views of policymakers or outside analysts.

Defense officials and outside experts have pointed to surveys like this one as evidence that policy discussions should incorporate more systematically gathered input from military professionals, who often have insights into operational readiness that are not always reflected in public statements from senior leadership.

## Context

The joint Foreign Policy–CNAS effort reflects a broader trend of using large-scale survey research to gauge institutional sentiment within the armed forces, supplementing traditional reporting and hearings with quantitative data drawn directly from officers themselves.

---

*Note: This article synthesizes general findings attributed to the survey; readers seeking specific statistics, direct quotations, or the precise publication date should consult the original Foreign Policy/CNAS report for full and exact figures.*

# Survey: U.S. Officers See China, Iran as Long-Term Winners of Iraq War

A recent survey of U.S. military officers has surfaced a striking consensus among the officer corps: many believe that China and Iran, not the United States, emerged as the primary strategic beneficiaries of the Iraq War.

## Key Findings

According to officers who participated in the survey, the extended U.S. military commitment in Iraq—which spanned the better part of a decade and consumed enormous resources, attention, and political capital—created openings that rival powers were well-positioned to exploit.

**On Iran:** Officers pointed to the removal of Saddam Hussein's government as fundamentally altering the regional balance of power in Tehran's favor. With a hostile Sunni-led government eliminated and a Shia-majority political system established in Baghdad, Iran gained significant influence over its western neighbor—influence that has persisted through political, economic, and militia networks in the years since.

**On China:** Respondents suggested that the sustained focus on counterinsurgency and stabilization operations in Iraq diverted American strategic attention, defense investment, and diplomatic bandwidth away from the Indo-Pacific during a critical period of Chinese economic and military expansion. While U.S. forces were engaged in Iraq, officers noted, Beijing had greater latitude to expand its economic reach, modernize its military, and assert territorial claims with less friction from Washington.

## Officer Sentiment

The survey suggests a degree of frustration or reflection within military ranks about opportunity costs—the idea that resources, readiness, and strategic focus devoted to Iraq came at the expense of countering what many officers now view as more consequential long-term competitors.

This perspective aligns with a broader post-war reassessment that has circulated in defense and foreign policy circles: that the Iraq War, whatever its stated objectives, may have inadvertently strengthened the hand of two nations now regarded as America's principal strategic rivals.

## Context

Such findings reflect an ongoing reckoning within the U.S. military establishment about the lessons of the Iraq War, particularly as national security priorities have shifted toward great-power competition with China and continued tension with Iran. The survey adds to a body of commentary from military professionals questioning whether the war's costs—in lives, money, and strategic focus—were commensurate with its outcomes.

# Survey Reveals Deep Concerns Among Military Personnel Over Iraq War's Strategic Toll

*By CNN Staff*

A comprehensive new survey of active-duty service members and military families has surfaced troubling data on troop morale, readiness concerns, and widespread skepticism about the long-term strategic value of the Iraq war, sparking renewed debate among lawmakers, Pentagon officials, and defense analysts.

## Key Findings on Morale

The survey, which polled thousands of service members across multiple branches, found that a significant portion of respondents reported declining morale tied directly to the frequency and duration of deployments. Repeated combat tours—some service members reporting three or more rotations—were cited as a primary driver of fatigue, strain on family life, and diminished confidence in mission clarity.

Respondents frequently pointed to the ambiguous nature of counterinsurgency operations, difficulty distinguishing combatants from civilians, and uncertainty about tangible progress as factors eroding unit cohesion and personal motivation. A notable percentage indicated they were less likely to reenlist than they had been earlier in their service, raising alarms about long-term retention in an all-volunteer force already stretched thin.

## Readiness Under Strain

Military analysts reviewing the data emphasized readiness implications extending beyond individual morale. The survey highlighted concerns about equipment attrition, delayed maintenance cycles, and insufficient dwell time between deployments—the rest period intended to allow troops and units to retrain, recover, and prepare for future contingencies.

Several senior officers quoted in supplementary interviews warned that the operational tempo required to sustain simultaneous commitments in Iraq and Afghanistan has left the broader force less prepared to respond to emerging threats elsewhere. National Guard and Reserve components, increasingly relied upon for active deployments, reported particular strain, with equipment shortages affecting units' homeland response capabilities as well.

## Perceptions of Strategic Impact

Perhaps the most striking element of the survey concerns troops' own assessments of how the Iraq war has shaped U.S. global standing. A substantial number of respondents expressed doubt that the war had strengthened America's broader strategic position, with many citing concerns that resources and attention diverted to Iraq had come at the expense of other priorities, including counterterrorism efforts elsewhere and relationships with allies.

Some respondents voiced worry that the prolonged engagement had emboldened adversaries or complicated U.S. diplomatic leverage in the region, while others noted skepticism about whether the war's original objectives—linked to weapons of mass destruction and regional stability—had been realized in ways that justified the human and financial costs.

## Reactions From Washington

The findings quickly became fodder for political debate. Members of the Senate Armed Services Committee called for hearings to further examine retention and readiness figures, with some lawmakers arguing the data underscores the need for troop reductions or a revised withdrawal timeline. Others cautioned against drawing sweeping policy conclusions from survey data alone, urging a broader review incorporating classified assessments from combatant commanders.

Pentagon spokespeople acknowledged the pressures identified in the survey but pushed back against characterizations suggesting a readiness crisis, pointing to ongoing initiatives aimed at increasing dwell time, expanding mental health resources, and modernizing equipment procurement to address wear from sustained operations.

## Broader Implications

Defense policy experts note that morale and readiness surveys, while not definitive predictors of institutional health, often serve as early indicators of deeper structural stress. The latest results add to a growing body of evidence suggesting that the human and material costs of extended conflict are becoming a central factor in debates over future U.S. military engagement strategy—not just in Iraq, but in shaping doctrine for any future large-scale, extended deployments.

As the debate continues, both supporters and critics of current war policy agree on one point: the perspectives of those who have served multiple deployments deserve serious weight in shaping the path forward, whether that means troop drawdowns, extended commitments, or a fundamental reassessment of strategic priorities in the region.

*CNN's coverage of military and defense policy will continue as more details from the survey and subsequent congressional hearings become available.*
